302.title: The fall (CCC 390, 404–405)
302.hook: a wound handed down to all, a loss of original holiness
302.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that baptism takes away original sin, while its wound, the inclination to sin, remains, and they turn to confession and grace for healing throughout life. The Exsultet, with its felix culpa, is sung at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, imago Dei: every human being made to the image of God. Your line was someone, not something. Today: if every person is God's image, why are people like this?

You promised yourself you wouldn't say it, and you said it. You meant to be patient, and the moment the kid spilled the juice, you weren't. Paul, writing to the Romans, describes it: the good he wants to do, he doesn't do, and the thing he hates, he does. Nobody has to teach a toddler to grab. Nobody takes a class in resentment. Something in people leans the wrong way before they've chosen anything. The Church has a name for that lean, and a story for where it came from. Today: the fall.
screen: `YOU SAID IT ANYWAY.` → `NOBODY TEACHES A TODDLER TO GRAB.` → `WHERE DOES THE LEAN COME FROM?`

segments.voice: First, the story. In Genesis 3, the first man and woman live in friendship with God in the garden. The serpent asks a question that plants doubt, and they reach for the one fruit they were told to leave. Then they hide. The Catechism says the account uses figurative language, but tells of a real event at the beginning of human history: the first people chose themselves over God. Second, what was lost. The Church calls it original holiness and justice: harmony with God, inside the person, between man and woman, and with creation. Paul sums it up in the Douay-Rheims: "Wherefore as by one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death." Third, original sin, the Catechism teaches, is contracted, not committed: a state people are born into, not a personal fault. No baby is guilty of anything it chose. Fourth, human nature is not totally corrupted. It is wounded: weakened in its powers, subject to ignorance, suffering and death, and inclined to sin. That inclination has an old name, concupiscence. Christians describe this in different ways: Orthodox Christians often speak of ancestral sin, many Reformed Protestants of a deeper corruption of nature, and the Catholic Church says wounded. And on Easter night, the Church sings an old Latin hymn that dares to call Adam's sin a happy fault, felix culpa, because of the one it brought to the rescue. So the Catholic story isn't about how bad people are, but about a wound that can be healed.
screen: `THEY REACHED, THEN HID.` · `ORIGINAL HOLINESS, LOST.` · `CONTRACTED, NOT COMMITTED.` · `WOUNDED, NOT TOTALLY CORRUPTED.` · then, large: `O FELIX CULPA.`

segments.voice: Look at one weakness of yours, a place where you lean the wrong way again and again, the way a good doctor looks at a wound: honestly, and with care, without defending it or beating yourself up. Then look the same way at someone else's weakness, one that grates on you. If you pray, you can ask for healing, for them and for you.
Original sin. Not a sin you committed, but a wound handed down to every human being from the beginning: the loss of original holiness, and a lean toward sin. Today's word.
Your line: wounded, not ruined. True of everyone, you included. Day three hundred two, done.

303.title: The Word was made flesh (CCC 456–460)
303.hook: God became human to save us, show us love, and share his life
303.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, Catholics bow during the Creed at the words about the Incarnation, and on Christmas and the Annunciation they genuflect at those words instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, original sin: a wound handed down, not a crime committed. Your line was wounded, not ruined. Today, the Church's answer to the wound.

Sunday Mass. The whole church is standing, saying the Creed together, words that are easy to say on autopilot. Then, midway, something strange happens. At one line, heads go down. People bow. On Christmas and on the feast of the Annunciation, they do more: they drop to one knee, right there in the pew, mid-sentence. Kids who don't know why do it because the grown-ups do. The line is about God doing something no one expected. Today: the Word made flesh.
screen: `THE CREED, ON AUTOPILOT.` → `EVERY HEAD GOES DOWN.` → `ONE KNEE, MID-SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The line is this: and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. First, the word. Incarnate comes from the Latin caro, carnis: flesh, the same root as carnivore and chili con carne. Incarnation means, bluntly, God in meat and bone. John's Gospel says it in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." The Word is the eternal Son, who was with God and was God, and he took flesh. Second, why. The Catechism gives four reasons, worth counting on your fingers. One: to save us, by reconciling us with God. Two: so that we might know God's love, which John says was shown by God sending his Son. Three: to be our model of holiness, a life you can actually watch. Four: to make us, in the words of Second Peter, partakers of the divine nature. Third, that last one surprises people. The Catechism quotes Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, who put it in one bold line: the Son of God became man so that we might become God. Theologians call it divinization. It doesn't mean people stop being creatures; it means God's life can be given to them. Fourth, the name. Matthew's Gospel calls the child Emmanuel, "which being interpreted is, God with us." Not God above, looking down. God with skin, who got hungry, tired, and thirsty. That's why heads bow in the Creed: it's the moment Catholics remember that the distance between God and people was crossed from God's side.
screen: `CARO: FLESH.` · `SAVE, SHOW LOVE, MODEL, SHARE.` · `THAT WE MIGHT SHARE GOD'S LIFE.` · `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · then, large: `AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: If you know the Creed, say it slowly to yourself, and at was incarnate, bow your head, or, if you're able and it feels right, go down on one knee, the way the Church does at Christmas; if you don't, just say the six words: and the Word was made flesh. Then stay there and notice your own flesh, your hands, your breath, the weight of your body: what Catholics say God took on.
Incarnation. From the Latin for flesh: the Son of God taking a real human body and soul, to save us, show us love, and share his life. Today's word.
Your line: god with skin. Hunger, tiredness, thirst: the Church's claim is that God has felt them too. That's day three hundred three.

304.title: True God and true man (CCC 464–469)
304.hook: fully God and fully human, not a mixture
304.howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ is true God and true man, and some meditate on his human feelings in the Gospels, especially in Lent and in the Sorrowful Mysteries of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Incarnation: the Word made flesh. Your line was god with skin. Today: how can one person be both?

One person, both God and human. The mind reaches for a shortcut. Maybe he was God wearing a human costume, like a king in disguise. Maybe a very holy man God adopted. Maybe half and half, like a centaur, or a blend, like coffee with milk, where you can't find either one anymore. Versions of those shortcuts were tried in the early Church and argued over in councils and letters, and the Church said no to them. What it said instead fits in five words.
screen: `A KING IN DISGUISE?` → `HALF AND HALF?` → `COFFEE WITH MILK?`

segments.voice: The council's word: Chalcedon. First, not part and part. The Catechism is plain: Jesus is not partly God and partly human, and not a confused mixture of the two. He is fully both. Second, the councils. In the year 451, bishops met at Chalcedon and wrote the careful version: one person, the Son of God, in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Four withouts, each closing a door on a shortcut. Some ancient churches, like the Coptic and Armenian churches, have put the faith in different words, and in recent decades their leaders and the popes have signed statements saying they share the same faith in Christ. Third, what fully human means: a human body, and also a human mind that learned, a human will, and human feelings. The Gospels don't hide them. In Mark, he looks around at people "with anger, being grieved for the blindness of their hearts." A rich man runs up and kneels before him, and Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. In the garden, he says: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." And at his friend Lazarus's tomb, in John, three plain words: "And Jesus wept." Fourth, why it matters. The letter to the Hebrews says Christians don't have a high priest who can't feel what they feel, but "one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The loneliness, the grief, the anger at unfairness, the dread before something hard: Catholics say none of it is foreign to him.
screen: `NOT PART AND PART. NOT A BLEND.` · `CHALCEDON, 451: FOUR WITHOUTS.` · `ANGER, LOVE, SORROW, TEARS.` · `TEMPTED IN ALL THINGS, WITHOUT SIN.` · then, large: `AND JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Pick one of the four moments, the anger at hard hearts, the love for the rich man, the sorrow in the garden, the tears at the tomb, and picture his face. Then find the same feeling somewhere in your own week, a time you were angry at something unfair or grief caught you, and set your moment next to his. If you pray, you can talk to him about it, as someone who knows.
Chalcedon, the council in 451 that defined Jesus as one person, truly God and truly human, without confusion or division. Today's word.

305.title: The Paschal mystery (CCC 571)
305.hook: his death and resurrection as one saving event
305.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Paschal mystery above all in the Easter Triduum, from Holy Thursday evening through Easter Sunday; at the Easter Vigil the Paschal candle is blessed, marked with a cross, alpha and omega, the year and five grains of incense, and lit from a new fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon: one person, fully God and fully human. Your line was he felt what you feel. Today, what he went through for it.

Late on Holy Saturday night, a Catholic church is dark. Outside, a fire burns in a small iron bowl. A priest cuts a cross into a tall new candle, then the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and the numbers of the year. He may press in five grains of incense, for five wounds. The candle is lit from the fire and carried into the dark, and one by one every small candle is lit from it, until the whole room is gold. A cross, wounds, and light, all on one candle. Catholics refuse to separate them.
screen: `A DARK CHURCH. A FIRE OUTSIDE.` → `A CROSS CUT INTO A CANDLE.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM GOES GOLD.`

segments.voice: Paschal comes from pascha, the Greek form of the Hebrew pesach: Passover. Jesus died at Passover, and the first Christians read his death through it. Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." The lamb whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the night of passing from slavery to freedom: Christians saw Jesus as that lamb, and his death and rising as that passage. One event, not two. The Catechism calls the cross and the resurrection together the Paschal mystery, and puts it at the center of the Good News. Good Friday isn't a sad chapter followed by a happy one. It's one saving act: through death to life. That's why the liturgy treats Holy Thursday evening to Easter Sunday as one great celebration, the Triduum, the three days. Mystery. In Catholic language, a mystery isn't a puzzle to solve. It's something true and so deep you can keep entering it your whole life without reaching the bottom. The pattern. Jesus gave it a picture beforehand: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Catholics say they are drawn into the Paschal mystery through baptism, and they recognize its shape in their own lives: endings that turn out to be passages, losses that bear fruit. Not every sorrow feels that way while you're in it, and the Church doesn't pretend it does. It points at the candle: the cross is still on it, even in the light.
screen: `PASCHA: PESACH, PASSOVER.` · `ONE EVENT: THE CROSS AND THE RISING.` · `A MYSTERY YOU KEEP ENTERING.` · `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT MUST DIE.` · then, large: `CHRIST OUR PASCH IS SACRIFICED.`

segments.voice: If you have a crucifix and a candle nearby, set them side by side; if not, picture them, and look at the cross, then the light, then both at once. Think of one ending in your own life that later became a beginning, a move, a loss, a no that led somewhere, and let it sit between the two. If you pray, you can thank God for it.
Paschal mystery. Christ's death and resurrection as one saving passage, named for the Passover, at the center of the Catholic faith.
Your line: through death to life. One passage, not two separate events. See you tomorrow.

306.title: If Christ be not risen (1 Corinthians 15:14; CCC 639)
306.hook: Catholics hold the resurrection happened, not as a metaphor
306.howItsDone: Catholics profess every Sunday in the Creed that Christ rose on the third day, celebrate the resurrection for the fifty days of Easter, and in many communities, especially Eastern Catholic ones, greet each other at Easter with Christ is risen, and the reply, he is truly risen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paschal mystery: the cross and the rising as one passage. Your line was through death to life. Today, the second half of that passage, and one very blunt sentence.

Word reaches the man who founded the church in Corinth: some members are saying the dead don't really rise. He could soften it. Say the story is beautiful, whatever happened. Say what matters is what Jesus taught. Instead he writes one of the bluntest sentences you could put in a letter: if it didn't happen, our preaching is empty, and so is your faith. He bets everything on one event. The writer is Paul, the letter is First Corinthians, and the Catholic Church still stands behind his bet.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` → `HE BETS EVERYTHING ON ONE EVENT.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And if Christ be not risen again, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." Vain means empty. Paul goes further: if Christ isn't raised, Christians are still in their sins, and if their hope is for this life only, they are of all people the most miserable. Then the witnesses. Just before this, Paul lists who saw the risen Jesus: Cephas, that's Peter, then the apostles, then more than five hundred people at once, many of whom, he says, are still alive. That detail reads like an invitation: go and ask them. And Paul says he is handing on what he himself received, so the list was already being passed along before he wrote it down. The Catechism calls the resurrection a real event, with manifestations that were historically witnessed, as the New Testament shows. Not a metaphor for the disciples' hope, not a way of saying his teaching lived on. The tomb was empty, and he was seen. And the Catechism points out that the disciples were not easy believers: they thought the women's report was nonsense, and Thomas refused to believe unless he could touch the wounds. What kind of rising? Not a return to the old life, the way Lazarus came back and would later die again. Catholics say Jesus rose into a glorified life that death can't touch: still bearing the wounds, able to eat with friends, no longer bound by locked doors. And in Matthew, the angel at the empty tomb answers Paul's if in three words: he is risen.

If you pray, you can bring the doubt and the joy to God together.
Egerthe, the Greek word the angel uses at the empty tomb: he was raised, he is risen. Paul's whole bet on one event.

307.title: The Holy Spirit (CCC 683–690)
307.hook: the advocate and comforter, the breath of the Church
307.howItsDone: Catholics call on the Holy Spirit with the prayer that begins come, Holy Spirit, and with the hymns Veni Creator Spiritus and Veni Sancte Spiritus; they celebrate the Spirit's coming at Pentecost and receive the Spirit's gifts in confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, egerthe: he is risen, Paul's bet on one event. Today, what the risen Jesus gives his friends when they're hiding behind a locked door.

Picture a courtroom. You're on trial, and you don't speak the language. Everyone talks fast, the papers make no sense, and you're completely alone. Then someone walks in, sits down beside you, puts a hand on your shoulder, and says: I'm with you. I'll speak for you. The night before he died, Jesus promised his friends someone exactly like that, using a Greek word from the courtroom. And after he rose, he gave that someone to them in the most intimate way imaginable: with his own breath.
screen: `ALONE IN A COURTROOM.` → `SOMEONE SITS DOWN BESIDE YOU.` → `GIVEN WITH A BREATH.`

segments.voice: At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete, that he may abide with you for ever." Paraclete is the Greek parakletos: someone called to your side. In a law court, an advocate. In grief, a comforter. English Bibles have tried both words, and neither holds all of it. Notice the word another. Jesus has been their Paraclete; now a second one is coming, who won't leave. Then the breath. On Easter evening the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. Jesus stands among them, and John says "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost." In both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit is also the word for breath and wind: ruach, pneuma. The Bible's first breath is God breathing life into the first human. Here the risen Jesus breathes again, and a new creation starts. How is the Spirit known? The Catechism says the Spirit is the one who lets anyone say Jesus is Lord at all, and yet he doesn't speak of himself. Catholics say they know him by what he does: in the Scriptures he inspired, in the sacraments, in prayer, in the gifts given to ordinary believers, and in the lives of the saints. And the Son and the Spirit, the Catechism says, are always sent together; you don't get one without the other. Catholics say the Spirit is the reason the Church is alive at all, the way breath is the reason a body is.
screen: `ANOTHER PARACLETE, FOR EVER.` · `HE BREATHED ON THEM.` · `KNOWN BY WHAT HE DOES.` · `THE SON AND THE SPIRIT, SENT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Notice your breath without changing it: every breath you've ever taken was given, not made. If you don't, simply breathe, and think of someone who once sat down beside you when you were alone.

308.title: Grace (CCC 1996–2005)
308.hook: a free gift, God's own life shared with us
308.howItsDone: Catholics believe sanctifying grace is first given in baptism and is restored and strengthened through the sacraments, especially confession and the Eucharist; some also pray for the actual graces they need for a particular day or task.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paraclete: the one called to your side, given with a breath. Your line was the breath of god. Today, what that breath brings with it.

Someone pays for your coffee in the drive-through line and drives off before you can thank them. What happens next varies. Some people want to pay it back, or pay it forward right away, or explain why they didn't really need it. A gift that can't be repaid takes the account out of your hands. Catholics say the life of God in the soul is exactly that kind of gift.
screen: `SOMEONE PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `PAY IT BACK? PAY IT FORWARD?` → `A GIFT YOU CAN'T REPAY.`

segments.voice: Grace is the Latin gratia, and you can hear its cousin in gratis: free. The Greek is charis, a gift freely given. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." What is the gift? The Catechism calls grace favor: the free and undeserved help God gives. Then it goes further. Grace is a share in God's own life. Not a thing God hands over from a distance: God giving himself. The Church names two kinds. Sanctifying grace, today's word, is a lasting gift that makes a person holy and a friend of God, first given in baptism. Actual graces are God's help in particular moments: the nudge to call someone, the strength to hold your tongue. One is like the life of a tree; the other, like the rain on a given day. And earning? Since the Reformation, Catholics and Protestants have argued about grace and merit, sometimes bitterly. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying together that people are accepted by God by grace alone, in faith in Christ, not because of any merit of their own. Catholics still speak of merit, and the Catechism explains that even merit is itself God's gift. A prayer of the Mass, drawing on Augustine, puts it this way: when God crowns our merits, he is crowning his own gifts.
screen: `GRATIA, GRATIS: FREE.` · `A SHARE IN GOD'S OWN LIFE.` · `THE TREE'S LIFE, THE DAY'S RAIN.` · `1999: BY GRACE ALONE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `IT IS THE GIFT OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something good in your life you did nothing to deserve: the family you were born into, a friend who stayed, your eyes, this morning's light. Don't explain it or plan how to pay it back; just receive it, the way you'd open your hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you.
Sanctifying grace. The lasting gift of God's own life, first given in baptism, that makes a person holy and a friend of God. Free, not earned.

Your line: free, not earned. From the fall to the Word made flesh, Chalcedon, the Paschal mystery, the resurrection, the Spirit, and now grace: that was the week. Day three hundred eight, a full week.
